A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with the same title, authors and sequential mean-estimation objective. All 41 pages of v3 and 46 pages of v4, including appendices, support comparison. Relocated material and renumbered results can be matched.

before.justification: Appendix A, Figure 2 reports original simulations using beta-distributed vectors and beta/binomial mixtures, including standard deviations across 100 trials.

after.justification: Appendix D, Figure 3 retains those original simulations. Figures 1–2 additionally report numerical comparisons of confidence-bound widths.

M1.justification: V4 replaces the von Mises–Fisher constructions with uniform distributions for the sub-ψ, time-varying-mean and empirical-Bernstein bounds, changing their computable formulas and tuning parameters. It also introduces a stitched Catoni–Giulini construction in Theorem 3.8. The underlying Catoni–Giulini truncation estimator is retained.

E1.justification: V4 Figure 1 adds numerical evaluation of sub-Gaussian bounds across covariance regimes. The task remains sequential mean estimation, and the bounded beta/binomial simulation coverage is retained. Newly discussed theoretical distribution classes do not constitute additional evaluated datasets.

E2.justification: V4 expands the earlier median-of-means comparison by adding geometric median-of-means (Minsker, 2015) alongside tournament median-of-means, and evaluates doubling variants as well as naive union bounds. Hsu et al. (2012), previously discussed theoretically, becomes an evaluated comparator in Figure 1. The empirical-Bernstein oracle comparators are retained.

E3.justification: The heavy-tail comparison changes from identity-covariance curves for d = 5, 20 and 100 through t = 10,000 to comparisons through t = 100,000, including matched trace and second-moment bounds of 5. These are revised comparison settings. V4 Figure 1 remains ambiguously specified: its caption gives covariance trace 5, whereas Appendix C gives 1 for the left panel.

E4.justification: V4 adds a covariance-ratio sensitivity analysis identifying regimes favorable to Hsu’s doubled bound, together with stitched versus unstitched comparisons. The earlier heavy-tail dimension sweep is removed. Figure 2’s enlarged GMoM panel redisplays a subset of the comparison rather than adding a separate analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions report standard-deviation shading across 100 trials for the retained empirical-Bernstein simulations. No new seed information, replication counts, significance tests or uncertainty-reporting practice is documented for the added numerical bound comparisons.

E6.justification: New sub-Gaussian curves show the stitched bound outperforming the unstitched bound, while Hsu with doubling can be tighter at small covariance ratios. Revised heavy-tail comparisons show GMoM sometimes beating unstitched Catoni–Giulini, while stitched Catoni–Giulini dominates the plotted alternatives. These are added or reworked comparisons, not controlled cross-version performance gains. The empirical-Bernstein plots are identical.

T1.justification: V4 revises the sub-Gaussian assumption to permit adapted covariance processes and replaces the vMF-based derivations. Sub-Gaussian and sub-gamma stitching already existed in v3 Appendix B; v4 strengthens those bounds and adds explicit sub-exponential, log-concave and Catoni–Giulini stitching proofs. It also adds Hsu-comparison and covariance-spectrum lemmas, and re-derives the empirical-Bernstein bound and its asymptotic width.

C1.justification: The abstract newly claims optimality, and the introduction and conclusion foreground explicit iterated-logarithm guarantees across additional cases. The auxiliary vMF contribution is dropped. V4 also explicitly advertises applicability beyond log-concavity to bounded Orlicz norm, although the underlying norm condition already appeared in v3 Theorem 2.

C2.justification: V4 adds explanations connecting Hsu’s competitiveness to covariance-spectrum terms and tournament MoM’s practical weakness to large constants. It discusses the distinction between knowing variance and knowing a raw second-moment bound, and compares the applicability of Orlicz-based and isotropic sub-exponential bounds. Principal limitations concerning known bounds and heavy-tail assumptions remain.

D1.justification: New Appendix C supplies a code-repository reference, explicit weighting and tuning choices, comparator formulas, and error allocations for union-bound and doubling constructions. V3 offered theoretical tuning advice but no corresponding simulation-details appendix or code-access statement. These are substantial documentation additions; the repository’s availability was not externally checked.

R1.justification: V4 adds Minsker (2015) and Lee et al. (2024), removes vMF-related references, and refines its comparisons with Hsu, Manole–Ramdas and Duchi–Haque. The central PAC-Bayesian positioning remains. The Waudby-Smith et al. 2021-to-2024 reference change identifies the same work’s publication update.

P1.justification: The title and main Introduction–Light tails–Heavy tails–Summary organization remain. V4 makes focused explanatory rewrites, removes the vMF interlude, reorganizes the appendices, adds a simulation-details section and adopts section-based theorem numbering. Much of the existing exposition is retained.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains rows and LIL/fixed-time-optimization columns. V4 adds a two-panel sub-Gaussian figure and replaces the heavy-tail inset with a larger two-panel comparison. The empirical-Bernstein figure moves unchanged, while the vMF illustration disappears. Several new plot legends retain obsolete theorem numbers, creating cross-reference inconsistencies.

improvement.justification: V4 substantially strengthens v3’s coarse stitched guarantees and limited comparative evidence through sharper explicit bounds, additional proofs, and stronger Hsu/GMoM/doubling comparisons that reveal both advantages and unfavorable regimes. Appendix C materially improves reproducibility information. These gains outweigh the Figure 1 covariance-setting contradiction and obsolete plot labels, which still impair reproducibility and clarity.
